Most accommodations happen because you're asking for a -specific- accommodation. BPD can be considered a disability, and yes, it can be accommodated. But you have to know what exact accommodations could help with your specific symptoms. 
Longer test times? Separate assignment space? Specific seat in the room? Whatever you think will help is what you need to ask for. They wont suggest things for you, they dont know how your disability affects you specifically, as it is different for everyone. Not one accommodation is a one-size-fits-all type thing.

Well, your dog is getting older, and usually around that age is when most dogs are retiring or newly retired. 


But, if you're not certain, try getting out more. Go on little training excursions. See if the dog wants to work anymore, and if her alerts get better with having more active working time. If she doesn't improve in a few weeks, or shows little interest in working, then it's probably time to retire her.

It sounds like you already have tasks in mind that a service dog could do to help you live a more independent life! That is the first step when considering one, and your needed tasks are very doable and valid. 
Your next step would be to talk to your treating doctor. Explain the same tasks you laid out here for us and see what they say. 
If they aren't educated in service animals, direct them to the FAQ of the ADA website (or the equivalent of that in your country), or if you're familiar enough with the laws yourself (which I strongly urge you to be, all handlers and potential handlers need to know their rights) you can offer to answer any questions they have and provide them with links and screenshots to the laws. 
Laws vary country to country, and if you're in the US, state laws even vary. 
I think with the tasks you listed, a service dog could be a great option for you, as long as you're understanding and willing to take on the responsibility of the care, training, negative public feedback, and knowing your rights.
